oewn-00767694-v.learner: to push or drive someone or something in the direction you point them.
examples: Mrs. Jenkinson was chiefly employed in watching how little Miss de Bourgh ate, pressing her to try some other dish
they were all pressed to go into the house and take some refreshment

oewn-00761702-v.learner: to ask for something, or to request it, in a strong and serious way.
examples: I am not so selfish, however, as to press for it, if inconvenient.
He confessed himself obliged to leave the regiment on account of some debts of honour which were very pressing

oewn-00795447-v.learner: to make someone willing to do something, or to lean them toward it, or to draw them to it.
examples: Mr. Bingley had not been of age two years when he was tempted, by an accidental recommendation, to look at Netherfield House.
she was tempted, by the pleasantness of the morning, to stop at the gates and look into the park

oewn-01811496-v.learner: to be so attractive or so inviting that someone starts to want it.
examples: We know how little there is to tempt anyone to our humble abode.

oewn-00784574-v.learner: to get someone to do something by promising things or by talking them round, when the promises are often false or bigger than the truth.
examples: my friend Denny tempted me further by his account of their present quarters, and the very great attentions

connotation.why: treats the persuasion as possibly false or overblown

examples: Mr. Bingley had danced with her twice, and she had been distinguished by his sisters.
I spoke to him twice myself without receiving an answer

oewn-00083743-r.learner: to double the amount or degree.
examples: The second box was twice as heavy as the first.

oewn-05146359-n.learner: the fact of not being good enough, or of falling short of being perfect.
examples: You never see a fault in anybody.
I have faults enough, but they are not, I hope, of understanding.

oewn-00071785-n.learner: a wrong act that comes from poor judgment, from not knowing, or from not paying attention.
examples: The clerk's one fault was writing the wrong date on the letter.

oewn-04677049-n.learner: being the one who is answerable when something bad happens.
examples: It was not her fault that the carriage came so late.

oewn-01864034-a.learner: kept for certain people or groups only, or giving people privacy.
examples: private balls are much pleasanter than public ones
May I hope, madam, for your interest with your fair daughter Elizabeth, when I solicit for the honour of a private audience with her
She kept her private opinion of the plan to herself.

oewn-01772598-s.learner: having to do with one person only.
examples: Each guest was given a private room with a desk in it.

oewn-02309241-a.learner: not changing or varying, above all in the way someone behaves.
examples: Between him and Darcy there was a very steady friendship, in spite of a great opposition of character.
nothing is to be done in education without steady and regular instruction

oewn-01997735-s.learner: showing firm determination that nothing can shake.
examples: Steady to his purpose, he scarcely spoke ten words to her through the whole of Saturday

connotation.why: approves of the firmness that a word like obstinate would fault

oewn-02102822-s.learner: firmly in place and not wobbling.
examples: He held the ladder steady while she climbed.

oewn-04763427-n.learner: the fact of being likely, or a thing that is likely to happen, or the thing most likely to happen.
examples: deliberated on the probability of each statement--but with little success
Most earnestly did she labour to prove the probability of error

oewn-05098974-n.learner: a measure of how likely an event is, given as a number that compares the cases which bring it about with all the cases that could happen.
examples: The probability of drawing a red card from a full deck is one half.

oewn-14429977-n.learner: the feeling of being irritated or annoyed.
examples: Elizabeth blushed and blushed again with shame and vexation.
Kitty was the only one who shed tears; but she did weep from vexation and envy.

oewn-07533500-n.learner: anger that comes from something irritating.
examples: His vexation at the long delay came out in a sharp reply.

oewn-05840588-n.learner: a thing or a person that makes you anxious or unhappy.
examples: general disappointment is only warded off by the defence of some little peculiar vexation

oewn-01793315-v.learner: to annoy someone again and again, over and over.
examples: whose blind partiality provoked her
I was sometimes quite provoked; but then I recollected my dear Elizabeth and Jane, and for their sakes had patience with her.

oewn-00795741-v.learner: to give something the push it needs to happen.
examples: which immediately provoking Elizabeth to do it, she turned to him and said

oewn-01763170-v.learner: to bring out a feeling or an answering reaction in someone.
examples: The news provoked laughter from everyone at the table.

oewn-01716563-v.learner: to do an action, or to carry it out.
examples: allow me to follow the dictates of my conscience on this occasion, which lead me to perform what I look on as a point of duty
She was confident of having performed her duty

oewn-01718067-v.learner: to play, sing, or act something for people who are watching or listening.
examples: Your friend performs delightfully
We neither of us perform to strangers.

oewn-02379855-v.learner: to carry out the job that something or someone is there to do.
examples: In the body, the liver performs several functions at once.
